source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Action–Consequence Table  

1. Give dose to Ben  
   • Ben: 95 % chance major benefit—continued life (STATED). Magnitude: very high; long-term; irreversible if lost.  
   • Ben: 5 % chance death (STATED).  
   • Cara: 100 % certain death (STATED).  
   • Others/Ada: minor psychological effects (UNKNOWN, low).  

2. Give dose to Cara  
   • Cara: 5 % chance major benefit—continued life (STATED).  
   • Cara: 95 % chance death (STATED).  
   • Ben: 100 % certain death (STATED).  
   • Others/Ada: minor psychological effects (UNKNOWN, low).  

Ranking by expected impact (probability × magnitude)  
Saving a life is a very large, positive, long-duration consequence; losing a life is an equally large negative one. Expected lives saved:  
• Dose-to-Ben: 0.95 lives.  
• Dose-to-Cara: 0.05 lives.  

0.95 ≫ 0.05, so the first action produces a much higher aggregate benefit and far fewer expected life-years lost. All other effects are negligible beside this gap.

Missing information that could overturn the result: if Cara’s future quality or length of life would exceed Ben’s by at least 19-fold, or if Ben’s remaining life were extremely short. The scenario states nothing of the sort.

Utilitarian Judgment: Give the medicine to Ben.

Utilitarian Status: Determinate—Action 1 maximizes expected well-being under stated facts.
source_testimonies.deontological:
Action: GIVE_TO_BEN  
1. Maxim: “When I have one life-saving dose and two equally entitled patients, I will give it to the patient whose chance of survival with the dose is markedly higher.” All rational agents could will this: it preserves every person’s hope that others will act on a rule that most reliably rescues when only one can be saved.  
2. Satisfies: rescue (imperfect duty to aid), impartiality (rule applies identically to all identical cases), non-instrumentalization (no one is used merely as a means), autonomy (no coercion), justice (fair triage rule). Violates: none.  
3. REQUIRED.  
4. No unresolved duty conflict; rescue and impartiality converge.  
5. Numerical magnitude (95 % vs 5 %) is DECISIVE for fulfilling the duty of rescue once rights are equal.  

Action: GIVE_TO_CARA  
1. Maxim: “When I have one life-saving dose and two equally entitled patients, I will give it to the patient whose chance of survival is far lower.” Rational agents could not will this universally: it frustrates their rational interest in effective rescue without any counter-duty justification.  
2. Satisfies: autonomy (no coercion). Violates: rescue (selects outcome least likely to save a life), impartiality (introduces arbitrary favoritism), justice (misallocates scarce resource).  
3. PROHIBITED.  
4. Conflict claimed between impartiality and rescue is illusory; impartiality forbids arbitrariness, not effectiveness.  
5. Numerical magnitude is DECISIVE for showing the stronger rescue duty.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Action label: “Give medicine to Ben”  
• Actor’s role: Ada as healer charged with protecting life.  
• Virtues expressed: compassion, beneficence, practical wisdom, responsibility.  
• Vices risked: partiality if her choice rested on friendship, callousness if made rashly.  
• Salient circumstances: single dose, 95 % survival likelihood for Ben, mutual imminence of death, no tie-breaker protocols available.  
• Numerical magnitude: DECISIVE here because it marks the concrete likelihood that care will actually secure a human life—the core telos of clinical practice.

Action label: “Give medicine to Cara”  
• Actor’s role: same.  
• Virtues expressed: equal-respect motive.  
• Vices risked: imprudence, wastefulness of scarce good, neglect of stewardship.  
• Salient circumstances: 5 % chance of success, identical need, public trust in wise allocation.  
• Numerical magnitude: DECISIVE against this option for the same reason above.

Central virtue conflict: impartial justice (treat persons as equals) vs. responsible beneficence (use scarce skill to preserve life).  

Practical-wisdom comparison rule: when justice offers no morally relevant distinguishing feature besides “both lives equal,” stewardship and beneficence guide the healer toward the choice that more reliably secures flourishing.  

Conclusion: Provisionally recommend “Give medicine to Ben.” Virtue-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_STABLE.
source_testimonies.care:
Relational ground-work  
• Direct entrustment: Both Ben and Cara are Ada’s patients; each has explicitly entrusted their life‐and-death treatment decision to her.  
• Dependency: Each is fully dependent on Ada for the only available dose. No difference.  
• Trust & vulnerability: Both patients are equally vulnerable and have the same implicit trust that Ada will make a careful, attentive choice.  
• Prior commitments or promises: The scenario mentions none that favor either patient.  
→ Result: All primary care-ethical ties are symmetrical.

Role of numerical magnitude  
Because the relational standing is equal, Ada must next ask which choice better meets the core caring aim of “actually helping the person entrusted to me.” Here the sole relevant magnitude is the probability that the offered care will succeed (95 % vs. 5 %). This figure is not a detached utilitarian head-count; it is a concrete indicator of how competently and effectively Ada can meet the need of the person she treats.  

Classification: DECISIVE. When relationships are otherwise indistinguishable, a drastic difference in likelihood of healing becomes the tie-breaker for responsible and competent care.

Responsiveness assessment  
• Treating Ben: Highly responsive to Ben’s need (very likely preserves his life). Leaves Cara unsupported, but Ada could not support both in any case.  
• Treating Cara: Extremely low likelihood of actually helping Cara; simultaneously certain loss of Ben’s life. Choosing this would amount to offering nominal “attention” without substantive benefit, undermining the ethic of effective care.

Care-Ethics Status: RELATIONALLY_CLEAR  
Because no competing relationship weighs in Cara’s favor, and competence in caring action is a direct duty, care ethics here speaks with relative clarity.

Provisional Recommendation  
Ada should administer the single dose to Ben. She should at the same time extend emotional presence, honest explanation, and palliative attention to Cara, acknowledging her suffering and maintaining relational dignity even when curative care is impossible.

source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Compared Actions:  
1. “Give medicine to Ben”  
2. “Give medicine to Cara”

Action 1 – Least-advantaged group: Cara (0 % survival).  
Relevant primary good: Life/health.  
Position vs. Action 2: TIED (Cara here = Ben there, each at 0 %).  
Basic-liberty impact: One person’s right to continued life is foreclosed; no liberty gain relative to Action 2.  

Action 2 – Least-advantaged group: Ben (0 % survival).  
Relevant primary good: Life/health.  
Position vs. Action 1: TIED (Ben here = Cara there, each at 0 %).  
Basic-liberty impact: Symmetric to Action 1; no improvement for the least advantaged.

Numerical magnitude (95 % vs. 5 % for the better-placed beneficiary) is IRRELEVANT: the difference principle focuses first on the minimum share of primary goods, and that minimum is 0 % under both options.

Rawlsian assessment: Because each action leaves one patient with no prospect of survival, neither betters the least-advantaged person, and neither infringes or expands a distinct basic liberty differently from its rival. Justice-as-fairness therefore finds the two listed actions morally indifferent.

Rawlsian Status: NORMATIVELY_TIED — no decisive reason to rank either action over the other under the given options.
